questions.challenge_mechanism: The three levels look additive, so the obvious method is to weight each level's own access time by its own hit rate and add the three products. That charges the level 2 hit time to every reference and main memory to almost none, because the weights are conditional rather than marginal: level 2 is consulted only on the 0.06 of references that miss in level 1, and main memory only on the 0.012 that miss in both. The error is invisible in the arithmetic, which is correct at every step, and it only surfaces when the two configurations are compared.
questions.question: A design team is comparing two memory configurations for a new single-core processor. The figure shows the proposed hierarchy. Every instruction fetch and every data read or write that the processor issues is presented to the level 1 cache first. A reference that misses in level 1 is passed to the level 2 cache, and a reference that also misses there is passed to main memory. The hit rate of each cache is the proportion of the references presented to it that it satisfies, and the time given for each level is the number of processor cycles that level adds when it is consulted. Registers are not part of the calculation. The team must decide whether the level 2 cache earns the die area it occupies, because that area could be given to other parts of the processor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average number of cycles the processor spends on one memory reference when both caches are present. Show clearly how the level 1 hit time, the level 2 hit time and the main memory access time each contribute to your total, and state the fraction of references that reach main memory.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the average number of cycles per memory reference if the level 2 cache is removed, so that every level 1 miss is passed directly to main memory. Give your answer to three significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the contribution that main memory makes to the average in part (a) is so much smaller than its access time of 150 cycles would suggest, and why the level 2 cache makes a larger contribution than its own hit rate alone implies.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate the proposal to remove the level 2 cache in order to recover its die area. Refer to your results from parts (a) and (b), and consider the effect on the processor's performance rather than only on the cost of manufacturing it.

questions.answer:
(a) The level 1 miss rate is $1 - 0.94 = 0.06$ (M1). Of those misses only $1 - 0.80 = 0.20$ are not satisfied by level 2, so the fraction of all references that reach main memory is $0.06 \times 0.20 = 0.012$, that is 1.2 per cent (A1).

The level 1 cache is consulted by every reference and adds 3 cycles, so its contribution is 3 cycles. The level 2 cache is consulted only by the 0.06 of references that miss in level 1 and adds 14 cycles to each of them, so its contribution is $0.06 \times 14 = 0.84$ cycles. Main memory is consulted only by the 0.012 of references that miss in both caches and adds 150 cycles to each of them, so its contribution is $0.012 \times 150 = 1.8$ cycles (A1).

The average number of cycles per reference is therefore $3 + 0.84 + 1.8 = 5.64$ cycles (A1).

(b) With no level 2 cache every level 1 miss is passed straight to main memory, so main memory is consulted by the whole 0.06 of misses and adds 150 cycles to each of them. Its contribution becomes $0.06 \times 150 = 9$ cycles (M1), and the average becomes $3 + 9 = 12.0$ cycles (A1). Removing the level 2 cache therefore raises the average from 5.64 to 12.0 cycles, a factor of $12.0 \div 5.64 = 2.13$ (A1).

(c) Main memory contributes only 1.8 cycles even though a single access costs 150 cycles, because it is reached by 1.2 per cent of references and by no others. Its 150 cycles are paid once per reference that misses in both caches, so multiplying 150 by the overall miss rate of 0.012 gives the average cost per reference; multiplying it by anything closer to 1 would charge the whole of main memory's latency to references that never reach it (M1).

The level 2 cache contributes more than its own hit rate suggests because its hit rate is conditional. The figure states that 0.80 of the references presented to level 2 are satisfied there, but only 0.06 of all references are ever presented to it, so the level 2 cache removes $0.06 \times 0.80 = 0.048$ of all references from the path to main memory (A1). Those references would otherwise have cost 150 cycles instead of 14, so the cache saves $0.048 \times (150 - 14) = 6.53$ cycles per reference; equivalently, comparing parts (a) and (b), it saves $12.0 - 5.64 = 6.36$ cycles (A1). A hit rate is a property of the cache, not of the program, and the two must be multiplied to obtain the share of references the cache actually rescues.

(d) The proposal should be rejected on performance grounds. Removing the level 2 cache raises the average memory reference from 5.64 to 12.0 cycles, an increase of 6.36 cycles on every reference the processor issues, which is a slowdown of about 2.13 times on any part of the workload that is memory-bound (A1). Because the level 2 cache is consulted on only 6 per cent of references but converts each of those from a 150-cycle main memory access into a 14-cycle access, it removes roughly 6.5 cycles per reference from the average while occupying far less die area than the level 1 cache does (A1).

The evaluation is not settled by cost alone. Die area given to level 2 could raise the level 1 hit rate instead, but part (a) shows that the level 1 hit time is paid by every reference and the level 1 miss rate is already only 0.06, so a further improvement there can remove at most 0.06 of the references from the level 2 path; the level 2 cache is currently rescuing 0.048 of them (A1). A design that removed level 2 would also make the processor's performance far more sensitive to the level 1 hit rate, because every additional level 1 miss would then cost the full 150 cycles rather than 14 (A1).

A justified answer must therefore weigh the 2.13 times slowdown against the area recovered, and should note that the decision depends on how memory-bound the intended workload is: a workload that fits in level 1 would lose little, while one that streams through data would lose most of its throughput (A1). Merely asserting that caches are fast, or that removing a component reduces cost, earns no credit.
questions.markscheme_notes:
Part (a) is marked for the conditional weights, not for the final number. Award M1 for the level 1 miss rate 0.06, then A1 for the joint miss rate 0.012, A1 for the three contributions being 3, 0.84 and 1.8 cycles, and A1 for the total 5.64.

A candidate who computes $0.94 \times 3 + 0.06 \times 14 = 3.66$ has weighted level 2 by the level 1 miss rate, which is correct, but has omitted main memory entirely; this is the commonest error and should be given M1 only.

A candidate who computes $0.94 \times 3 + 0.80 \times 14 + 0.012 \times 150$ has weighted level 2 by its own unconditional hit rate. The arithmetic is right and the reasoning is wrong; award M1 for the level 1 term and M1 for the main memory term, but no A1 for the total.

Part (b) expects 12.0 cycles and the factor 2.13. Accept 2.1. A candidate who writes 9 cycles for main memory but forgets to add the 3 cycles of level 1 hit time scores M1 only.

Part (c) needs both directions: main memory is small because it is rarely reached, and level 2 is large because its hit rate is conditional on a level 1 miss. One direction only scores M1.

Part (d) is an evaluation and must engage with the numbers. A bare recommendation with no reference to 5.64, 12.0 or 2.13 scores no more than M1. Award the remaining marks for recognising that the level 2 cache is cheap in area relative to the level 1 cache, and for noting that the answer depends on the workload.
questions.explanation:
The item is built on a conditional-probability structure that is disguised as a sum. Three levels are drawn in a pyramid, each with a hit rate and a time, and the shape invites the reader to weight each time by the hit rate printed beside it and add. That is the trap. The hit rate of the level 1 cache is unconditional, because every reference is presented to it, but the hit rate of the level 2 cache is conditional on having missed in level 1, and main memory has no hit rate at all because it always answers. The three numbers are therefore not the same kind of quantity and cannot be combined by the same rule.

The consequence is a factor-of-two error in the answer that decides the question. A candidate who weights level 2 by 0.80 obtains $0.94 \times 3 + 0.80 \times 14 + 0.012 \times 150 = 15.8$ cycles, which makes the level 2 cache look as though it were adding 11.2 cycles to every reference rather than 0.84. A candidate who weights level 2 by 0.06 but forgets main memory obtains 3.66 cycles, which is too small. Both errors are arithmetically clean, so neither is caught by checking the working; only the conditional structure catches them.

Part (b) is the payoff. Computing the average again without level 2 gives 12.0 cycles, so the cache is worth 6.36 cycles per reference and a factor of 2.13 in average access time. A candidate carrying the 15.8 figure forward would instead conclude that removing the cache costs almost nothing, because 15.8 already contains the 11.2 that the cache was wrongly charged with. The evaluation in part (d) therefore cannot be answered correctly unless part (a) is right, which is what makes the arc work: the opening part carries the idea and the closing part tests whether it was understood.

The figure is load-bearing rather than decorative. The hit rates and the three times are printed only in the figure, the direction of the hand-off between levels is drawn only there, and the caption states that every reference is presented to level 1 first. Nothing in the stem repeats those numbers, so an answer cannot be produced without reading the diagram, which is the test STANDARD.md 4.3.1 sets for a figure.

provenance.adaptation: Three changes. Context: a design review deciding whether to keep a second-level cache, rather than a textbook exercise that asks for an average access time with no decision attached. Given and asked: the hit rates and times are given only in a figure, so the conditional structure has to be read off the diagram rather than out of the stem, and the same hierarchy is costed twice so the two configurations can be compared. Reasoning chain: the final part asks for a judgement that is only defensible once the opening part is right, so an error in the weights propagates into the conclusion instead of being confined to a number.
provenance.resource_origin: UK A-level Computer Science and US AP Computer Science A: the memory hierarchy and the effect of cache on processor performance, where an average access time is computed from hit rates (structure adapted; the hierarchy, all rates and all times are original)

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Weight each level's own access time by the hit rate printed beside that level in the figure, add the three products, and report the sum as the average cycles per reference
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The level 2 hit rate is conditional on a level 1 miss and main memory is reached only when both caches miss, so weighting the level 2 time by 0.80 charges eleven cycles to references that never consult level 2 at all
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: An average near 15.8 cycles per reference, which makes the level 2 cache appear to add 11.2 cycles to every reference and makes removing it look almost costless

verification.method: The two configurations are recomputed from the hit rates and times independently of the markscheme, the joint miss rate is checked both as a product and as the sum of the contributions, and the saving is confirmed to equal the difference of the two averages.
solution_skeleton: Read the two hit rates and the three access times out of the figure.
Multiply the level 1 miss rate by the level 2 miss rate to get the share reaching memory.
Weight each level's access time by the share of references that actually consult it.
Add the three contributions to obtain 5.64 cycles per reference.
Repeat the calculation with main memory reached by every level 1 miss to obtain 12.0.
Compare the two averages to obtain the factor of 2.13 and judge the proposal.

figure.caption: Two captured frames, each with the 8-bit sum and the carry-out produced by the receiver's adder.

questions.challenge_mechanism: The carry-out of an adder is the obvious overflow test because it is the one bit the hardware makes visible, and on one of these two frames it agrees with the truth. The frames are chosen so that it disagrees in both directions: frame A produces a carry-out while its signed result is correct, and frame B produces no carry-out while its signed result is wrong. A candidate who checks the carry bit is right once for the wrong reason and wrong once without noticing.
questions.question: A sensor network transmits each measurement as a three-byte frame. The first byte is the reading and the second is a calibration offset, and both are 8-bit two's complement values; the third byte is a checksum. Two frames captured from the network are shown in the figure, together with the 8-bit sum that the receiver's adder produced for each of them and the carry-out bit that the same adder produced. The receiver must reject any frame whose two signed values cannot be added without the result being misrepresented, and the engineer who wrote the receiver used the carry-out bit to make that decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the signed decimal value of the reading and of the offset in frame A, and state the true arithmetic sum of those two values. Show how the first bit of each byte is used in your decoding.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Deduce the signed decimal value that the 8-bit sum in frame B represents, and state with a reason whether the addition of the two signed values in frame B has overflowed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the checksum of each frame from its first two bytes, and state whether each of the two checksums in the figure is correct.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the carry-out bit cannot be used to decide whether a signed addition has overflowed. Your answer should refer to both frames and should state the condition that does detect overflow.

questions.answer:
(a) In frame A the first byte is 0x7A, which in binary is 0111 1010. Its leading bit is 0, so the value is positive and the remaining bits give $64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 = 122$ (A1). The second byte is 0x9C, which is 1001 1100. Its leading bit is 1, so it is negative, and its magnitude is found by taking the two's complement: $1001\,1100 \to 0110\,0011 \to 0110\,0100$, which is $64 + 32 + 4 = 100$ (A1). The offset is therefore $-100$.

The true arithmetic sum of the two signed values is $122 + (-100) = 22$ (A1). Because the two values have opposite signs, the sum lies between them and no overflow is possible.

(b) In frame B the first byte is 0x6F, which is 0110 1111 with a leading bit of 0, so the reading is $+111$. The second byte is 0x32, which is 0011 0010 with a leading bit of 0, so the offset is $+50$ (M1). Their true sum is $111 + 50 = 161$, which is greater than the largest value an 8-bit two's complement number can hold, namely $+127$ (A1).

The 8-bit sum shown in the figure is 0xA1, which is 1010 0001. Its leading bit is 1, so it represents a negative number, and its magnitude is $0101\,1110 + 1 = 0101\,1111 = 95$, giving $-95$ (A1). Adding two positive values has produced a negative result, so the addition has overflowed.

(c) The checksum is the exclusive OR of the first two bytes. For frame A, $0111\,1010$ XOR $1001\,1100 = 1110\,0110$, which is 0xE6 (M1) (A1). The figure shows 0xE6, so the checksum of frame A is correct (A1).

For frame B, $0110\,1111$ XOR $0011\,0010 = 0101\,1101$, which is 0x5D (M1). The figure shows 0x5D, so the checksum of frame B is also correct (A1). This matters: the frame that overflows is not corrupt, and a receiver that relied on the checksum alone would accept it.

(d) The carry-out is the bit that leaves the most significant position of the adder, and it reports whether the unsigned sum of the two bit patterns exceeded 255. That is not the same question as whether the signed sum exceeded 127 or fell below $-128$, because the same bit patterns mean different things under the two interpretations (A1).

Frame A shows the first failure. Its bytes are 0x7A and 0x9C, whose unsigned values are 122 and 156. Their unsigned sum is 278, which exceeds 255, so the adder produces a carry-out of 1. The signed values, however, are 122 and $-100$, whose sum is 22 and fits comfortably; the carry-out is 1 while there is no overflow (A1). A receiver that rejected on the carry-out would discard a good frame.

Frame B shows the opposite failure. Its bytes are 0x6F and 0x32, whose unsigned values are 111 and 50. Their unsigned sum is 161, which does not exceed 255, so the carry-out is 0. The signed values are $+111$ and $+50$, whose sum of 161 exceeds 127, so the result stored is $-95$ and the addition has overflowed (A1). A receiver that accepted on the carry-out would accept a frame whose value is wrong by 256.

Overflow for signed addition is detected from the signs of the operands and the sign of the result, not from the carry-out: overflow occurs when two operands of the same sign produce a result of the opposite sign (A1). Equivalently, it is the exclusive OR of the carry into the most significant position and the carry out of it. In frame A the signs are opposite, so no overflow is possible whatever the carry-out is; in frame B both operands are positive and the result is negative, so overflow has occurred whatever the carry-out is (A1).
questions.markscheme_notes:
Part (a): award A1 for decoding 0x7A as +122 with the leading bit used as the sign, A1 for decoding 0x9C as $-100$ by taking the two's complement of the magnitude, and A1 for the true sum 22. A candidate who reads 0x9C as 156 or as $-28$ has not applied two's complement and scores no marks on the second point.

Part (b): M1 for reading both bytes as positive, A1 for identifying that 161 exceeds +127, and A1 for decoding 0xA1 as $-95$. Accept $-95$ with or without the working.

Part (c): M1 for the exclusive OR method and A1 for each correct checksum. The marks are for the method and the values; a candidate who XORs the three bytes together, or who adds rather than XORs, scores no marks here.

Part (d): this is the discriminating part. A1 for stating that the carry-out answers the unsigned question rather than the signed one, A1 for frame A as the false-rejection case, A1 for frame B as the false-acceptance case, and A1 for the correct rule that overflow is detected from the signs of the operands and the result. A candidate who asserts that overflow occurs when the carry-out is 1 without noticing frame B scores at most A1.

Note that both checksums are correct, so the checksum cannot be used to detect the overflow either; a candidate who says the frame is corrupt has misread the question.
questions.explanation:
The item separates two things that share a name. The carry-out bit and signed overflow are both described informally as the addition having gone past the end, and on many textbook examples they coincide, which is exactly why the carry-out is such a persistent error. The two frames here are chosen to break the coincidence in both directions, so the rule cannot be salvaged by adjusting it.

Frame A is the false-rejection case. Its two bytes are 0x7A and 0x9C. As unsigned patterns these are 122 and 156, summing to 278, so a carry-out is produced. As signed patterns they are 122 and $-100$, summing to 22, so nothing is wrong. The carry-out is 1 and there is no overflow. Frame B is the false-acceptance case. Its bytes are 0x6F and 0x32, which are 111 and 50 unsigned and also $+111$ and $+50$ signed. The unsigned sum is 161, which fits in eight bits, so there is no carry-out; the signed sum is 161, which does not fit, so the stored result of 0xA1 reads back as $-95$. The carry-out is 0 and there is an overflow.

Because the same hardware bit is wrong in both directions on the same item, a candidate who guesses cannot pass part (d) by pattern-matching on the first frame. The correct rule is stated in terms of the signs: overflow occurs when two operands share a sign and the result does not. It can also be expressed as the exclusive OR of the carry into and the carry out of the sign position, which is the form a hardware designer would use and which is why the single visible carry-out is not enough.

The checksum is a deliberate second layer. Both frames have correct checksums, so the third byte offers no help in detecting the overflow and a candidate who looks for corruption there finds none. This forces the answer back onto the interpretation of the two signed bytes, which is the point of the item.

The figure carries every value the answer needs, including the carry-out that the receiver's engineer relied on, so the trap is presented as data rather than described in the stem. The two frames are decoded from the same two's complement function in the generator that the markscheme uses, so the picture and the answer cannot drift apart.

provenance.adaptation: Three changes. Context: a receiver that must decide whether to accept a frame, rather than an exercise that asks only for the sum of two binary numbers. Given and asked: two frames are given and the carry-out of each is supplied in the figure, so the candidate has to decide whether that bit is the right test rather than being told that it is not. Reasoning chain: the final part requires the candidate to generalise from two cases that fail in opposite directions, so a rule fitted to one frame is visibly insufficient.
provenance.resource_origin: US AP Computer Science A and UK A-level Computer Science: two's complement representation, signed overflow and the carry-out bit (structure adapted; the two frames, all byte values and the checksum are original)

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Read the carry-out bit printed beside each sum and reject the frame whose carry-out is 1, because a carry out of the most significant position is taken to mean the result did not fit
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The carry-out answers the unsigned question while the frame stores signed values, so on frame A it is 1 with no overflow and on frame B it is 0 with an overflow that leaves the stored byte wrong by 256
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: Frame A rejected as unrepresentable and frame B accepted as valid, which is the exact inverse of the truth and would pass a receiver test written from a single textbook example

verification.method: Both frames are decoded and re-encoded from the same two's complement function, the carry-out is recomputed as the quotient of the raw sum by 256, and the overflow condition is checked independently from the signs of the operands and the result.
solution_skeleton: Decode each byte by reading its leading bit as the sign.
Take the two's complement of the magnitude when the leading bit is 1.
Add the two signed values and compare the result with the range -128 to +127.
Exclusive-OR the first two bytes to obtain each checksum.
Compare the carry-out with the sign change to separate the two notions.
State the sign rule: overflow needs operands of one sign and a result of the other.

questions.challenge_mechanism: Round-robin and first-come-first-served are usually compared by quoting a definition, and both are described as fair, so the comparison is settled by adjectives. Here the two schedules have to be traced and their averages computed, and the result is that round-robin wins on both measures, which is not what the usual slogan predicts. The trap is the short job: P3 needs one unit of processor time and arrives fourth, so under round-robin it waits behind a full quantum of P1, and its own waiting time is larger than P2's.
questions.question: A single-core processor runs three processes that are all held in the ready queue. The figure gives the arrival time and the burst time of each process, and the round-robin schedule that the scheduler produced with a time quantum of four units. The scheduler always adds a process that has just arrived to the back of the ready queue before it adds a process that has used its whole quantum, and a process that finishes inside its quantum is removed immediately. The operating system designer is choosing between this scheduler and a first-come-first-served scheduler, and wants to know which of the two gives the better average waiting time and which gives the better response for an interactive workload.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the completion time of each of the three processes under the round-robin schedule shown in the figure. Show the order in which the processes are dispatched and the length of each dispatch.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the waiting time of each process under this round-robin schedule and hence the average waiting time. Define the waiting time you use.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the average waiting time if the same three processes were scheduled first-come-first-served in order of arrival, and state which scheduler gives the smaller average.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate which of the two schedulers is more suitable for an interactive system, using your results and considering how the two schedulers behave when a long process arrives before a short one.

questions.answer:
(a) Under round-robin the ready queue is ordered by arrival, and each process runs for at most four units before returning to the back of the queue.

At time 0 only P1 has arrived, so P1 is dispatched and runs from 0 to 4, using a whole quantum and leaving 3 units of work (A1). P2 arrives at time 2 and P3 at time 4, so both are waiting when the quantum expires; P2 is added before P1 because P2 arrived first. P2 is dispatched from 4 to 8 and finishes inside its quantum, so it is removed at time 8 (A1). P3 is dispatched from 8 to 9, finishes inside its quantum, and is removed at time 9 (A1). P1 is dispatched again from 9 to 12 and finishes at time 12 (A1).

The completion times are therefore P2 at 8, P3 at 9 and P1 at 12.

(b) The waiting time of a process is the total time it spends in the ready queue, which is its completion time minus its arrival time minus its burst time.

For P1: $12 - 0 - 7 = 5$ units (M1). For P2: $8 - 2 - 4 = 2$ units (A1). For P3: $9 - 4 - 1 = 4$ units (A1).

The total waiting time is $5 + 2 + 4 = 11$ units, so the average is $11 \div 3 = 3.67$ units (A1).

Note that P3, the shortest process, has a longer waiting time than P2. It arrives at time 4, exactly when P1's first quantum expires, and P2 is placed ahead of it because P2 arrived earlier. This is a property of the queue order, not an error in the trace.

(c) First-come-first-served runs the processes to completion in order of arrival. P1 runs from 0 to 7 and finishes at 7 (A1). P2 runs from 7 to 11 and finishes at 11, so its waiting time is $11 - 2 - 4 = 5$ units (A1). P3 runs from 11 to 12 and finishes at 12, so its waiting time is $12 - 4 - 1 = 7$ units.

The total is $0 + 5 + 7 = 12$ units, so the average is $12 \div 3 = 4.00$ units (A1). Round-robin therefore gives the smaller average waiting time, 3.67 against 4.00.

(d) Round-robin is the more suitable scheduler for an interactive system, and the reason is the response time rather than the average waiting time. The response time of a process is the delay before it first receives the processor. Under round-robin P1 first runs at 0, P2 at 4 and P3 at 8, so the response times are 0, 2 and 4 units and the average is 2.0 units (A1). Under first-come-first-served P1 first runs at 0, P2 at 7 and P3 at 11, so the response times are 0, 5 and 7 units and the average is 4.0 units (A1). A user interacting with the system perceives the delay before the first response, so halving it is a substantial gain even though the two schedulers differ by only 0.33 units in average waiting time.

The behaviour when a long process arrives first is the decisive case. Under first-come-first-served a process that needs a long burst blocks every process behind it for the whole of that burst, so a short interactive job can be delayed by the full length of an unrelated long job; this is the convoy effect, and P3's waiting time of 7 units is a small example of it (A1). Round-robin bounds the delay before any waiting process is dispatched by one quantum, so a long job can delay a short one by at most the quantum rather than by its whole burst.

The cost of that bound is context switching, since every quantum boundary forces the processor to save one process and restore another, and a smaller quantum means more such switches (A1). Round-robin is therefore the better choice for interactivity, provided the quantum is large enough that the switching overhead stays small relative to the work done in a quantum.
questions.markscheme_notes:
Part (a): A1 for each of the four dispatches. Accept the completion times alone only if the dispatch order and the quantum lengths are shown; the marks are for the trace, not the three numbers.

The commonest error is to place P1 ahead of P2 when the first quantum expires, which produces completion times of 8, 9 and 12 in a different order and gives P1 a waiting time of 1. Award M1 for a self-consistent trace, but no A1 for the dispatch order.

Part (b): M1 for the definition of waiting time as completion minus arrival minus burst, A1 for P1 and P2, A1 for P3, A1 for the average 3.67. Accept 11/3. A candidate who uses turnaround time instead of waiting time obtains 7.67 and scores no A1, because the definition was asked for.

Part (c): A1 for each completion time and A1 for the average 4.00. A candidate who reuses the round-robin completion times here scores no marks.

Part (d): this part is about response time, not throughput. A1 for the response times 2.0 against 4.0, A1 for the convoy effect or the one-quantum bound, and A1 for the context-switching cost. A bare recommendation scores nothing; the evaluation must use the numbers.
questions.explanation:
Scheduling questions are usually answerable from a definition, because the marks are for naming the algorithm that suits a stated workload. This item makes the two candidate algorithms produce answers that are close enough that a slogan cannot separate them, and then asks a question whose answer is not the one the slogan predicts.

Round-robin gives an average waiting time of 3.67 units and first-come-first-served gives 4.00. The difference is small, and a candidate who reasons that first-come-first-served is unfair to short jobs would expect a larger gap. The reason the gap is small is that the trace itself has a surprise in it: P3, the shortest process, waits longer than P2, because it arrives exactly at the moment P1's first quantum expires and P2 has an earlier arrival time. The queue order, not the algorithm's reputation, determines that waiting time.

The part that separates the two schedulers properly is response time. Round-robin gives first responses at 0, 4 and 8, so the average is 2.0; first-come-first-served gives 0, 7 and 11, so the average is 4.0. Response time is what an interactive user experiences, and it is not the same quantity as waiting time, so a candidate who answers part (d) from the part (b) numbers alone will reach the right conclusion for the wrong reason and will not be able to say what the round-robin quantum is buying.

The convoy effect is the general statement of the difference. Under first-come-first-served a long burst delays everything behind it by its full length, so the worst-case delay is unbounded in the length of the longest job. Under round-robin the worst-case delay before a waiting process is dispatched is one quantum. That bound is what makes the algorithm suitable for interactive use, and it is paid for with context switches, which is the trade-off a complete answer names.

The figure is required for parts (a) to (c). The arrival and burst times appear only in the process table, and the round-robin schedule is drawn as a Gantt chart whose blocks give the dispatch order and the quantum boundaries directly. A candidate cannot trace the schedule without reading the chart, and the chart is generated from the same simulation the markscheme uses, so the drawn blocks and the quoted completion times cannot disagree.

provenance.adaptation: Three changes. Context: a designer choosing between two schedulers for a stated workload, rather than an exercise that asks for the average waiting time of a given schedule. Given and asked: only the round-robin schedule is drawn, so the first-come-first-served schedule has to be derived and the two then compared, and the part that decides the recommendation is response time rather than the waiting time that was computed first. Reasoning chain: the closing part asks for a judgement about interactivity that the waiting-time averages alone do not settle, so the candidate has to notice that a second measure is needed.
provenance.resource_origin: UK A-level Computer Science: processor scheduling, round-robin with a time quantum, and the comparison of scheduling algorithms (structure adapted; the process set, all timings and the trace are original)

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Trace the two schedules, report the two average waiting times, and recommend round-robin because its average is the smaller of the two by about a third of a unit
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The averages differ by only 0.33 units, which is too small to decide anything, and the quantity an interactive user actually experiences is the delay before the first response, where the gap is 2.0 against 4.0 units
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: A recommendation of round-robin supported only by 3.67 against 4.00, which cannot explain why the quantum matters or what would change if a long process arrived first

verification.method: The round-robin schedule is produced by simulating the ready queue rather than by hand, and the waiting, turnaround and response times are each recomputed from the completion and first-dispatch times; the first-come-first-served schedule is traced independently.
solution_skeleton: Read the arrival and burst times from the table in the figure.
Simulate the ready queue, dispatching each process for at most one quantum.
Record the completion time of each process from the Gantt chart.
Subtract arrival and burst times to obtain the three waiting times.
Trace the first-come-first-served schedule separately and average its waiting times.
Compare the response times to judge suitability for an interactive workload.
